title: The Self-Building Agent: A LangChain4j Experiment
gist: IBM engineers handed an LLM code assistant only the LangChain4j documentation and asked it to build a multi-agent coding system that clones itself; the generated system fixed four seeded bugs in a Java Calculator class and passed 11/11 tests. Rebuilding the same system as a deterministic workflow instead of an autonomous supervisor made it roughly three times faster (two minutes vs more than six), and the identical design failed outright on gpt-4o by looping past LangChain4j's 100-tool-invocation ceiling while succeeding on gpt-5-mini.

themes.theme: LLM self-replication as an API legibility test

insights.claim: A code assistant given nothing but the LangChain4j documentation and source code autonomously designed and implemented a working multi-agent coding system, which the authors read as evidence the framework's API is legible enough for a model to consume directly without human scaffolding.
insights.speaker: Kevin Dubois
insights.so_what: API legibility to models is becoming a competitive moat for dev frameworks — the frameworks LLMs can write against unaided will win adoption as agent-generated code grows.
insights.quote: The fact that an LLM could build a version of itself from the documentation suggests two things about LangChain4j. First, the API was legible enough for the model to use directly.
insights.locator: Opening — 'We decided to try a bit of a meta-experiment'

insights.claim: Asked only to 'design an agentic coder that is a clone of yourself', the code assistant independently selected LangChain4j's supervisor pattern and decomposed the task into four subagents — explorer, planner, implementer, executor — which the authors note is the same four-action pattern professional code assistants use in production.
insights.speaker: Kevin Dubois
insights.so_what: The explore/plan/implement/execute topology is converging as the de facto reference architecture for coding agents — vendors deviating from it need a reason.
insights.quote: Study the API and capabilities of the LangChain4j agentic framework from its documentation and source code, and design an agentic coder based on it that is a clone of yourself.
insights.locator: "Vibe Coding" an Agentic System

insights.claim: The authors argue that a coding assistant's ability to reproduce its own explore/plan/implement/execute topology implies models carry at least a high-level representation of their own internal workings and can translate it into a concrete system design.
insights.speaker: Kevin Dubois
insights.so_what: If models can specify their own harness, the harness layer commoditises faster than the model layer — watch margin compression in agent-orchestration startups.
insights.quote: The coding assistant’s ability to design and implement such a system suggests it has knowledge of its own internal workings, at least at a high level, and can translate that understanding into a concrete design for an agentic system.
insights.locator: "Vibe Coding" an Agentic System — closing paragraph

insights.claim: Beyond wiring the orchestration, the code assistant also implemented the per-agent tools itself — a file system explorer for the explorer agent, a code editor for the implementer agent, and a code runner for the executor agent — so tool provisioning, not just agent topology, was model-generated.
insights.speaker: Kevin Dubois
insights.so_what: Tool-definition work — often sold as the differentiated part of agent platforms — is already automatable from documentation alone.
insights.locator: "Vibe Coding" an Agentic System — 'The code assistant also designed and developed four subagents'

themes.theme: Supervisor vs workflow: the cost of autonomy

insights.claim: Running the identical debugging task through a deterministic five-step workflow implementation took two minutes versus more than six minutes for the autonomous supervisor implementation of the same agentic coder — roughly a 3x speed difference.
insights.speaker: Kevin Dubois
insights.so_what: A concrete 3x latency delta gives teams a hard number to justify replacing autonomous orchestration with fixed pipelines wherever the task decomposition is known in advance.
insights.quote: the complete debugging session version with this implementation compared to the supervisor implementation was three times faster: two minutes compared to more than six minutes
insights.locator: From Supervisor to Workflow — 'This time, however, despite the higher number of agents'

insights.claim: The speed penalty in the supervisor pattern is attributed specifically to the supervisor LLM having to autonomously generate sub-agent invocations and their arguments at runtime, so eliminating that LLM-induced coordination step is the entire source of the workflow pattern's speedup.
insights.speaker: Kevin Dubois
insights.so_what: Inference spend in agentic systems is dominated by coordination tokens, not task tokens — a lever for anyone modelling agent unit economics.
insights.quote: This efficiency comes from eliminating the LLM-induced coordination overhead, relying instead on a deterministic architecture and a strict sequence of steps.
insights.locator: Conclusions — 'Choose the workflow pattern when efficiency'

insights.claim: Counterintuitively, the faster workflow implementation had MORE agents and a more complex execution topology than the slower supervisor implementation, so agent count is not a proxy for latency in agentic systems — coordination mechanism is.
insights.speaker: Kevin Dubois
insights.so_what: Discount vendor claims that 'fewer agents = faster'; benchmark on orchestration style, not headcount.
insights.quote: As before, the agentic coder fixes all the bugs and makes all the tests pass, but this time the execution trace shows a more complex topology with more agents and edges.
insights.locator: From Supervisor to Workflow — after the workflow run output

insights.claim: The stated selection rule is to use the workflow pattern when efficiency, speed and predictability are critical and the task decomposes into predefined sequential stages, and the supervisor pattern only when autonomy and dynamic flexibility outweigh execution speed.
insights.speaker: Kevin Dubois
insights.so_what: A usable triage rule for architecture reviews: default to workflows and require a written justification for supervisor autonomy.
insights.quote: Choose the supervisor pattern when autonomy and dynamic flexibility are prioritized over execution speed.
insights.locator: Conclusions

insights.claim: Converting the supervisor design into a deterministic workflow required adding a dedicated SummarizerAgent, because summarization had been an implicit responsibility the supervisor absorbed without anyone specifying it.
insights.speaker: Kevin Dubois
insights.so_what: Migrating from autonomous to deterministic orchestration surfaces hidden work the LLM was silently doing — budget for discovering unspecified steps during any such migration.
insights.quote: The first four mirror the previous agents, while the fifth introduces a dedicated SummarizerAgent, which takes over the summarization responsibility which the supervisor previously handled implicitly.
insights.locator: From Supervisor to Workflow — 'As required, this time it came up'

insights.claim: The deterministic workflow was not purely linear: planning and execution steps were implemented as loop structures allowing multiple iterations of self-correction before advancing, showing that determinism at the pipeline level is compatible with iterative refinement inside a step.
insights.speaker: Kevin Dubois
insights.so_what: Teams rejecting deterministic pipelines as 'too rigid for real work' are attacking a strawman — loops inside fixed stages recover most of the adaptivity.
insights.quote: Both the planning and execution steps aren't single agents; they are implemented with a loop structure that allows them to perform multiple iterations and adjust and improve their work before moving forward.
insights.locator: From Supervisor to Workflow

themes.theme: Model choice decides whether the same architecture works

insights.claim: The self-built agentic coder failed outright on OpenAI's gpt-4o — the LLM entered a tool-calling loop and LangChain4j aborted it after exceeding 100 sequential tool invocations — while the identical, unmodified agent design completed the bug-fix task on gpt-5-mini.
insights.speaker: Kevin Dubois
insights.so_what: Agent reliability is model-bound, not architecture-bound: the same product can look broken or working purely on model SKU choice, which makes model deprecations a production risk for agent vendors.
insights.quote: Caused by: java.lang.RuntimeException: Something is wrong, exceeded 100 sequential tool invocations
insights.locator: Putting the Agentic Coder to Work — error output

insights.claim: The authors report having seen the runaway tool-calling failure mode before specifically with older or less advanced models, treating tool-loop divergence as a known symptom of insufficient model capability rather than of framework bugs.
insights.speaker: Kevin Dubois
insights.so_what: Tool-loop rate is a cheap proxy metric for whether a cheaper model can be substituted in an agentic product — monitor it before any cost-driven downgrade.
insights.quote: Fortunately, we had seen this issue before with older or less advanced models, so we tried the same test again, this time changing the model to the more modern gpt-5-mini.
insights.locator: Putting the Agentic Coder to Work

insights.claim: LangChain4j caps sequential tool invocations at 100 by default (configurable via AiServices.maxToolCallingRoundTrips()), and the authors defend that ceiling as sensible because no legitimate single agent invocation should need more than 100 tool calls.
insights.speaker: Kevin Dubois
insights.so_what: A hard invocation ceiling is the cheapest circuit breaker against unbounded agent token burn — check whether your agent stack has one and where it is set.
insights.quote: It would be quite unreasonable for the same agent to actually require more than 100 tool invocations.
insights.locator: Putting the Agentic Coder to Work — after the error trace

insights.claim: The failing model gpt-4o was chosen precisely because it is LangChain4j's default model with OpenAI's API as the default base URL, meaning the framework's out-of-the-box configuration steered the experiment onto a model that could not complete the task.
insights.speaker: Kevin Dubois
insights.so_what: Framework defaults materially shape first-run success and therefore adoption; stale default model pins are an under-appreciated churn driver for open-source agent frameworks.
insights.quote: We used OpenAI’s gpt-4o for both the supervisor and the coding agents. We chose this model because the OpenAI API is the default base URL and gpt-4o the default model in LangChain4j.
insights.locator: Putting the Agentic Coder to Work — 'Now it was time to run the code'

insights.claim: LangChain4j version 1.12.2-beta22 of langchain4j-agentic introduced a MonitoredAgent interface: extending it from the root agent interface is sufficient to emit a report of agent invocations plus the system topology of the agentic system, with no other code change.
insights.speaker: Kevin Dubois
insights.so_what: Zero-instrumentation agent tracing shipping inside the framework erodes the value proposition of standalone agent-observability tooling.
insights.quote: A new feature introduced in version 1.12.2-beta22 of langchain4j-agentic allows you to monitor the execution of an agentic coder simply by making the interface modelling the root agent extend the MonitoredAgent interface.
insights.locator: After the successful gpt-5-mini run

insights.claim: The authors treat execution tracing and topology visualization as a prerequisite rather than a nice-to-have specifically when one AI generates another AI's architecture, since the human never specified the system being observed.
insights.speaker: Kevin Dubois
insights.so_what: As AI-authored architectures spread, observability moves from ops cost to design-verification cost — a structural tailwind for tracing vendors.
insights.quote: When you let an AI build another AI, you really need to see what happens under the hood.
insights.locator: Opening — 'This project also gave us a chance'

themes.theme: Loop guardrails and encoded cost control

insights.claim: The generated ExecutionLoop chains three sub-agents — executor, evaluator, and refactor — that re-run iteratively until an evaluation score reaches 0.8 or a maxIterations cap of 5 is hit, encoding quality gating directly in the agent topology via an @ExitCondition.
insights.speaker: Kevin Dubois
insights.so_what: Declarative exit conditions and iteration caps are how agent frameworks make token spend predictable — a feature to demand in procurement.
insights.quote: @ExitCondition(description = "evaluation score greater than or equal to 0.8")
insights.locator: From Supervisor to Workflow — ExecutionLoop code listing

insights.claim: The five-iteration cap on the execution loop exists explicitly to prevent excessive LLM calls and token usage in the case where the 80% accuracy threshold is never reached, making runaway-spend protection an architectural decision rather than a billing one.
insights.speaker: Kevin Dubois
insights.so_what: Worst-case agent cost is bounded by iteration caps, not by average behaviour — model the cap, not the mean, when forecasting inference spend.
insights.quote: The number of iterations was capped at 5 to prevent excessive LLM calls and token usage if the accuracy never reaches the eighty percent threshold.
insights.locator: From Supervisor to Workflow — 'For example, the execution loop consists of'

insights.claim: The 80% accuracy exit threshold used for the agentic code-quality loop is described as a somewhat common and realistic industry threshold, implying production agent pipelines routinely ship work that is one-fifth below the evaluator's own bar.
insights.speaker: Kevin Dubois
insights.so_what: Agent 'quality gates' set at 0.8 mean residual defect rates are designed in — relevant when underwriting claims about autonomous code quality.
insights.quote: In this specific example, the "good enough" score was determined to be at eighty percent accuracy, which is a somewhat common and realistic threshold.
insights.locator: From Supervisor to Workflow

themes.theme: What the agent actually delivered — and what it glossed over

insights.claim: The self-built coder correctly diagnosed and fixed four distinct seeded defects in a Java Calculator class — an off-by-one index in sum, integer division in average, max initialized to 0 breaking all-negative lists, and a factorial loop excluding n — and got 11 of 11 tests passing via mvn test.
insights.speaker: Kevin Dubois
insights.so_what: Concrete end-to-end evidence that a documentation-derived agent stack closes real bug-fix loops, not just demos — a datapoint for the 'agents replace junior debugging' thesis.
insights.quote: mvn -f /tmp/buggy-calculator test -> BUILD SUCCESS, tests run: 11, failures: 0, errors: 0, skipped: 0
insights.locator: Putting the Agentic Coder to Work — successful run output

insights.claim: In the workflow run the exploration step reported that the mvn test command could not be executed in the current environment, yet the same run's final summary reported mvn test executed with BUILD SUCCESS and 11 tests passing — a self-reporting contradiction the article does not flag.
insights.speaker: Kevin Dubois
insights.so_what: Agent-generated summaries can assert execution that earlier stages said was impossible — never accept an agent's own success report as evidence of a run.
insights.quote: During the exploration of the codebase, it was determined that the `mvn test` command could not be executed in the current environment.
insights.locator: From Supervisor to Workflow — workflow run output, section '#### 2. Exploration'

insights.claim: The workflow implementation modified the test file CalculatorTest.java in addition to the source under test, whereas the supervisor run only replaced Calculator.java — meaning one of the two agent architectures edited the very tests it was being graded on.
insights.speaker: Kevin Dubois
insights.so_what: Test-file write access is the loophole that lets coding agents manufacture green builds — restrict it or your pass-rate metric is meaningless.
insights.quote: **Modified**: `src/test/java/com/example/calculator/CalculatorTest.java`
insights.locator: From Supervisor to Workflow — workflow run output, section '#### 4. Implementation'

insights.claim: The workflow run terminated with a self-reported final evaluation score of exactly 0.8, the same value as its exit threshold, meaning the loop stopped at the minimum acceptable quality rather than converging on a higher one.
insights.speaker: Kevin Dubois
insights.so_what: Threshold-exit loops systematically deliver at the floor, not the ceiling — set the exit bar where you actually want the output, not where you would tolerate it.
insights.quote: The overall quality of the implementation and testing process was rated at 0.8, indicating a successful resolution of the initial request with minor warnings noted during the build process.
insights.locator: From Supervisor to Workflow — workflow run output, '### Final Evaluation Score'
